question: Find the normative rules: what RFC 7519 (JWT), RFC 8725 (JWT Best Current Practices), RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice), RFC 7009 (token revocation), RFC 7662 (token introspection), RFC 9449 (DPoP), RFC 6749 / the OAuth 2.1 draft, RFC 10017 ("OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications", published August 2026, formerly the IETF draft of that name), and the cookie specification (RFC 6265 / RFC 6265bis / draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies), say with MUST / SHOULD / MAY about: where a browser-based client may keep tokens, refresh token rotation or sender-constraining for public clients, token lifetimes, validating exp / aud / alg, what a revocation endpoint must do and what it does to self-contained tokens, and cookie attributes. Must find: the exact clause, its modal verb and its conditions.

facts.summary: RFC 10017 says browser-based apps are expected to follow RFC 9700, and that it expands on and further restricts some RFC 9700 recommendations.
facts.quote: Many of these recommendations are derived from the Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security [RFC9700], as browser-based applications are expected to follow those recommendations as well. This document expands on and further restricts various recommendations given in [RFC9700].

facts.summary: In the BFF pattern, the BFF MUST set the Secure flag on its cookies.
facts.quote: The BFF MUST enable the Secure flag for its cookies.

facts.summary: The BFF MUST set the HttpOnly flag on its cookies.
facts.quote: The BFF MUST enable the HttpOnly flag for its cookies.

facts.summary: The BFF SHOULD (not MUST) set SameSite=Strict on its cookies.
facts.quote: The BFF SHOULD enable the SameSite=Strict flag for its cookies.

facts.summary: The BFF SHOULD use cookie path / and SHOULD NOT set a Domain attribute.
facts.quote: The BFF SHOULD set its cookie path to /. … The BFF SHOULD NOT set the Domain attribute for cookies.

facts.summary: The BFF SHOULD give its cookie a name prefix showing it was set over HTTP, for example the __Host-Http- prefix from the [COOKIES] reference.
facts.quote: The BFF SHOULD start the name of its cookie with a prefix indicating the cookie was set via HTTP, for example, by using the __Host-Http- prefix defined in [COOKIES].

facts.summary: The page explains the SHOULD cookie items are kept below MUST so that existing architectures can still comply.
facts.quote: The "SHOULD" items are not deemed as "MUST" items so that existing architectures can be compliant.

facts.summary: RFC 10017's [COOKIES] reference, where __Host-Http- is defined, is the Internet-Draft draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies-02 of 21 May 2026, listed as work in progress.
facts.quote: "Cookies: HTTP State Management Mechanism", Work in Progress, Internet-Draft, draft-ietf-httpbis-layered-cookies-02, 21 May 2026

facts.summary: When client-side sessions carry access tokens, the BFF SHOULD encrypt the cookie contents; the page notes encryption still lets an attacker replay the encrypted cookie.
facts.quote: when using client-side sessions that contain access tokens (as opposed to server-side sessions where the tokens only live on the server), the BFF SHOULD encrypt its cookie contents. … Note that while encrypting the cookie contents prevents direct access to embedded tokens, it still allows the attacker to use the encrypted cookie in a session hijacking attack.

facts.summary: The BFF MUST implement a CSRF defense; which mechanism fits depends on the domain the BFF is deployed on.
facts.quote: The BFF MUST implement a proper CSRF defense. The exact mechanism or combination of mechanisms depends on the exact domain where the BFF is deployed, as discussed below.

facts.summary: SameSite=Strict alone is an adequate CSRF defense only if no other application shares the BFF's site (eTLD+1).
facts.quote: This defense is adequate if the BFF is never considered to be same site with any other applications. However, it falls short when the BFF is hosted alongside other applications within the same site, defined as the eTLD+1

facts.summary: When relying on CORS against CSRF, the BFF SHOULD require a custom request header, and if it does, MUST check that every incoming request carries it.
facts.quote: the BFF SHOULD require that the browser-based application includes a custom request header. Cross-origin requests with a custom request header always require a preflight, which makes CORS an effective CSRF defense. When this mechanism is used, the BFF MUST ensure that every incoming request carries this static header.

facts.summary: The BFF defeats token theft from the browser because it exposes no tokens to the browser-based application.
facts.quote: The BFF counters the first two attack scenarios by not exposing any tokens to the browser-based application. Even when the attacker gains full control over the application, there are simply no tokens to be stolen.

facts.summary: The BFF architecture is strongly recommended for business, sensitive and personal-data applications.
facts.quote: This architecture is strongly recommended for business applications, sensitive applications, and applications that handle personal data.

facts.summary: For refresh tokens issued to browser-based apps, authorization servers MUST either rotate them on each use or sender-constrain them per RFC 9700 Section 4.14.2.
facts.quote: In particular, authorization servers: … MUST either rotate refresh tokens on each use OR use sender-constrained refresh tokens as described in Section 4.14.2 of [RFC9700]

facts.summary: Authorization servers MUST either cap a browser app's refresh token lifetime or expire it after a period of non-use.
facts.quote: MUST either set a maximum lifetime on refresh tokens OR expire if the refresh token has not been used within some amount of time

facts.summary: When a refresh token has a preset expiry, a rotated refresh token MUST NOT outlive the initial one.
facts.quote: MUST NOT, upon issuing a rotated refresh token, extend the lifetime of the new refresh token beyond the lifetime of the initial refresh token if the refresh token has a preestablished expiration time

facts.summary: Authorization servers SHOULD tie refresh token lifetime to the user's authorization server session, so logout invalidates refresh tokens issued to browser-based apps.
facts.quote: Authorization servers SHOULD link the lifetime of the refresh token to the user's authenticated session with the authorization server. Doing so ensures that when a user logs out, previously issued refresh tokens to browser-based applications become invalid, mimicking a single-logout scenario.

facts.summary: Storing a token in a cookie through the JavaScript Cookie API is NOT RECOMMENDED, because the browser also sends that cookie to the app's server.
facts.quote: Because of these unintentional side effects of using cookies for JavaScript-based storage, this practice is NOT RECOMMENDED.

facts.summary: localStorage gives no protection against malicious JavaScript running in the same origin.
facts.quote: localStorage does not protect against unauthorized access from malicious JavaScript, as the attacker would be running code within the same origin, and as such, would be able to read the contents of the localStorage.

facts.summary: Refresh token rotation does not stop an attacker who keeps the legitimate app from using the latest refresh token, because then no reuse is detected.
facts.quote: Refresh token rotation is not sufficient to prevent abuse of a refresh token. An attacker can easily ensure that the application will not use the latest refresh token. … Since the application will not use the latest refresh token, there will be no detectable refresh token reuse, giving the attacker full control over the stolen refresh token.

facts.summary: With a BFF, revoking the user's access and/or refresh token is stated to be enough to stop further access, without invalidating the cookie-based session.
facts.quote: It suffices to revoke the user's access token and/or refresh token to prevent ongoing access to protected resources, without the need to explicitly invalidate the cookie-based session.

facts.summary: DPoP with a non-extractable key pair in IndexedDB prevents an XSS attacker from exfiltrating usable tokens, but not from running a new flow for fresh tokens.
facts.quote: the private key used to sign DPoP proofs is handled by the browser (a non-extractable [CryptoKeyPair] is stored using [W3C.IndexedDB]). As a result, the use of DPoP effectively prevents scenarios where the XSS attacker exfiltrates the application's tokens (see Sections 5.1.1 and 5.1.2). … Note that the use of DPoP does not prevent the attacker from running a new flow to obtain a fresh access token (and optionally a refresh token); see Section 5.1.3.

facts.summary: The authorization server MUST NOT issue access tokens in the authorization response, and browser-based clients MUST NOT use the Implicit grant.
facts.quote: the authorization server MUST NOT issue access tokens in the authorization response and MUST issue access tokens only from the token endpoint. Browser-based clients MUST use the Authorization Code grant type and MUST NOT use the Implicit grant type to obtain access tokens.

facts.summary: Authorization and resource servers SHOULD sender-constrain access tokens, for example with mutual TLS (RFC 8705) or DPoP (RFC 9449).
facts.quote: Authorization and resource servers SHOULD use mechanisms for sender-constraining access tokens, such as mutual TLS for OAuth 2.0 [RFC8705] or OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP) [RFC9449] (see Section 4.10.1), to prevent misuse of stolen and leaked access tokens.

facts.summary: Refresh tokens of public clients MUST be sender-constrained or rotated; confidential clients' refresh tokens are already bound to the client by RFC 6749.
facts.quote: Refresh tokens for public clients MUST be sender-constrained or use refresh token rotation as described in Section 4.14. [RFC6749] already mandates that refresh tokens for confidential clients can only be used by the client for which they were issued.

facts.summary: Access tokens SHOULD be audience-restricted; a resource server MUST refuse a token not meant for it, and the aud claim MAY carry the restriction.
facts.quote: access tokens SHOULD be audience-restricted to a specific resource server or, if that is not feasible, to a small set of resource servers. … If it was not, the resource server MUST refuse to serve the respective request. The aud claim as defined in [RFC9068] MAY be used to audience-restrict access tokens.

facts.summary: Clients SHOULD NOT use the implicit grant or other responses that return access tokens in the authorization response, unless injection is prevented and the leakage vectors are mitigated.
facts.quote: clients SHOULD NOT use the implicit grant (response type token) or other response types issuing access tokens in the authorization response, unless access token injection in the authorization response is prevented and the aforementioned token leakage vectors are mitigated.

facts.summary: Authorization servers SHOULD make access tokens sender-constrained and audience-restricted, though some deployments may be unable to for architecture or performance reasons.
facts.quote: Authorization servers therefore SHOULD ensure that access tokens are sender-constrained and audience-restricted as described in the following. Architecture and performance reasons may prevent the use of these measures in some deployments.

facts.summary: Sender-constraining is undermined when an attacker obtains both the token and the key material, notably via XSS in a browser client.
facts.quote: Note that the security of sender-constrained tokens is undermined when an attacker gets access to the token and the key material. This is, in particular, the case for corrupted client software and cross-site scripting attacks (when the client is running in the browser).

facts.summary: Refresh tokens let the authorization server issue short-lived, reduced-scope access tokens, which limits the impact of access token leakage.
facts.quote: They also add to the security of OAuth, since they allow the authorization server to issue access tokens with a short lifetime and reduced scope, thus reducing the potential impact of access token leakage.

facts.summary: Authorization servers MUST decide by risk assessment whether to issue refresh tokens to a client, and issued refresh tokens MUST be bound to the consented scope and resource servers.
facts.quote: Authorization servers MUST determine, based on a risk assessment, whether to issue refresh tokens to a certain client. … If refresh tokens are issued, those refresh tokens MUST be bound to the scope and resource servers as consented by the resource owner.

facts.summary: For public clients, authorization servers MUST use one of the listed methods to detect refresh token replay; one is cryptographically binding the refresh token to a client instance (RFC 8705 or RFC 9449).
facts.quote: Authorization servers MUST utilize one of these methods to detect refresh token replay by malicious actors for public clients: … Sender-constrained refresh tokens: the authorization server cryptographically binds the refresh token to a certain client instance, e.g., by utilizing [RFC8705] or [RFC9449].

facts.summary: Rotation issues a new refresh token on each refresh and invalidates the old one; replay is detected only when both attacker and legitimate client use the token, and the server then revokes the active refresh token.
facts.quote: Refresh token rotation: the authorization server issues a new refresh token with every access token refresh response. The previous refresh token is invalidated, but information about the relationship is retained by the authorization server. If a refresh token is compromised and subsequently used by both the attacker and the legitimate client, one of them will present an invalidated refresh token, which will inform the authorization server of the breach. The authorization server cannot determine which party submitted the invalid refresh token, but it will revoke the active refresh token.

facts.summary: If the grant is encoded inside the refresh token, authorization servers MUST protect the token value's integrity, for example with signatures.
facts.quote: The grant to which a refresh token belongs may be encoded into the refresh token itself. … Authorization servers MUST ensure the integrity of the refresh token value in this case, for example, using signatures.

facts.summary: Authorization servers MAY automatically revoke refresh tokens on a security event such as a password change or logout at the authorization server.
facts.quote: Authorization servers MAY revoke refresh tokens automatically in case of a security event, such as: … password change or … logout at the authorization server.

facts.summary: Refresh tokens SHOULD expire after a period in which the client has not used them; the period is the authorization server's choice.
facts.quote: Refresh tokens SHOULD expire if the client has been inactive for some time, i.e., the refresh token has not been used to obtain fresh access tokens for some time. The expiration time is at the discretion of the authorization server.

facts.summary: RFC 7009 presents revocation as the way a client invalidates its tokens when the user logs out, changes identity or uninstalls the app.
facts.quote: This revocation mechanism allows a client to invalidate its tokens if the end-user logs out, changes identity, or uninstalls the respective application.

facts.summary: Implementations MUST support revoking refresh tokens and SHOULD support revoking access tokens.
facts.quote: Implementations MUST support the revocation of refresh tokens and SHOULD support the revocation of access tokens (see Implementation Note).

facts.summary: Revocation endpoint URLs MUST be HTTPS URLs.
facts.quote: URLs for token revocation endpoints MUST be HTTPS URLs.

facts.summary: The authorization server first validates the client credentials (for confidential clients), then checks that the token was issued to the requesting client, and refuses the request if that fails.
facts.quote: The authorization server first validates the client credentials (in case of a confidential client) and then verifies whether the token was issued to the client making the revocation request. If this validation fails, the request is refused

facts.summary: Invalidation is immediate, though a propagation delay between servers is possible; clients must not use the token after an HTTP 200 response.
facts.quote: The invalidation takes place immediately, and the token cannot be used again after the revocation. In practice, there could be a propagation delay, for example, in which some servers know about the invalidation while others do not. Implementations should minimize that window, and clients must not try to use the token after receipt of an HTTP 200 response from the server.

facts.summary: Revoking a refresh token SHOULD also invalidate all access tokens of the same grant if the server supports access token revocation; revoking an access token MAY also revoke its refresh token.
facts.quote: If the particular token is a refresh token and the authorization server supports the revocation of access tokens, then the authorization server SHOULD also invalidate all access tokens based on the same authorization grant (see Implementation Note). If the token passed to the request is an access token, the server MAY revoke the respective refresh token as well.

facts.summary: The endpoint answers HTTP 200 both when the token was revoked and when the submitted token is invalid.
facts.quote: The authorization server responds with HTTP status code 200 if the token has been revoked successfully or if the client submitted an invalid token.

facts.summary: Error code unsupported_token_type means the server does not support revoking the presented token type.
facts.quote: unsupported_token_type: The authorization server does not support the revocation of the presented token type.

facts.summary: The revocation endpoint MAY support CORS when it is meant for user-agent-based applications.
facts.quote: The revocation endpoint MAY support Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) [W3C.WD-cors-20120403] if it is aimed at use in combination with user-agent-based applications.

facts.summary: For self-contained access tokens, immediate revocation needs some backend interaction between authorization server and resource server, which the RFC calls currently non-standardized.
facts.quote: The access tokens may be self-contained so that a resource server needs no further interaction with an authorization server issuing these tokens to perform an authorization decision of the client requesting access to a protected resource. … In the former case, some (currently non-standardized) backend interaction between the authorization server and the resource server may be used when immediate access token revocation is desired.

facts.summary: For handle-style access tokens that refer to data at the authorization server, the server can revoke them because the resource server relays each token to it.
facts.quote: A system design may, however, instead use access tokens that are handles referring to authorization data stored at the authorization server. … In the latter case, the authorization server is able to revoke an access token previously issued to a client when the resource server relays a received access token.

facts.summary: An alternative is short-lived access tokens renewed with refresh tokens, which limits how long a revoked access token stays in use.
facts.quote: Another design alternative is to issue short-lived access tokens, which can be refreshed at any time using the corresponding refresh tokens. This allows the authorization server to impose a limit on the time revoked when access tokens are in use.

facts.summary: If the server does not support access token revocation, revoking the refresh token does not immediately invalidate access tokens.
facts.quote: If the authorization server does not support access token revocation, access tokens will not be immediately invalidated when the corresponding refresh token is revoked. Deployments must take this into account when conducting their security risk analysis.

facts.summary: A JWT processor that does not find itself in a present aud claim MUST reject the JWT; the aud claim itself is OPTIONAL.
facts.quote: If the principal processing the claim does not identify itself with a value in the "aud" claim when this claim is present, then the JWT MUST be rejected. … Use of this claim is OPTIONAL.

facts.summary: A JWT MUST NOT be accepted on or after its exp time; the current time MUST be before exp.
facts.quote: The "exp" (expiration time) claim identifies the expiration time on or after which the JWT MUST NOT be accepted for processing. The processing of the "exp" claim requires that the current date/time MUST be before the expiration date/time listed in the "exp" claim.

facts.summary: Implementers MAY allow a small clock-skew leeway for exp, usually a few minutes at most; exp is a NumericDate and is OPTIONAL.
facts.quote: Implementers MAY provide for some small leeway, usually no more than a few minutes, to account for clock skew. Its value MUST be a number containing a NumericDate value. Use of this claim is OPTIONAL.

facts.summary: A JWT MUST NOT be accepted before its nbf time, with the same optional small leeway.
facts.quote: The "nbf" (not before) claim identifies the time before which the JWT MUST NOT be accepted for processing. The processing of the "nbf" claim requires that the current date/time MUST be after or equal to the not-before date/time listed in the "nbf" claim.

facts.summary: The jti claim is a unique identifier that can be used to prevent replay of a JWT; it is OPTIONAL.
facts.quote: The "jti" claim can be used to prevent the JWT from being replayed. The "jti" value is a case- sensitive string. Use of this claim is OPTIONAL.

facts.summary: Which claims a JWT must contain to be valid depends on the context and is outside RFC 7519's scope.
facts.quote: The set of claims that a JWT must contain to be considered valid is context dependent and is outside the scope of this specification.

facts.summary: An Unsecured JWT is a JWS whose alg header is "none" and whose signature is the empty string.
facts.quote: An Unsecured JWT is a JWS using the "alg" Header Parameter value "none" and with the empty string for its JWS Signature value

facts.summary: If any JWT validation step fails, the JWT MUST be rejected.
facts.quote: If any of the listed steps fail, then the JWT MUST be rejected -- that is, treated by the application as an invalid input.

facts.summary: Allowed algorithms are an application decision; even a validly checked JWT SHOULD be rejected if its algorithms are not acceptable to the application.
facts.quote: Finally, note that it is an application decision which algorithms may be used in a given context. Even if a JWT can be successfully validated, unless the algorithms used in the JWT are acceptable to the application, it SHOULD reject the JWT.

facts.summary: Conforming JWT implementations MUST implement HS256 and "none"; RS256 and ES256 are RECOMMENDED.
facts.quote: only HMAC SHA-256 ("HS256") and "none" MUST be implemented by conforming JWT implementations. It is RECOMMENDED that implementations also support RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with the SHA-256 hash algorithm ("RS256") and ECDSA using the P-256 curve and the SHA-256 hash algorithm ("ES256").

facts.summary: A JWT's contents cannot be trusted unless cryptographically secured and bound to the context of the trust decision.
facts.quote: The contents of a JWT cannot be relied upon in a trust decision unless its contents have been cryptographically secured and bound to the context necessary for the trust decision.

conflicts.topic: may a browser client use the implicit grant?
conflicts.note: RFC 9700 says SHOULD NOT with an 'unless' exception; RFC 10017 says browser-based clients MUST NOT, with no exception (F1: RFC 10017 further restricts RFC 9700).
RFC 9700 says refresh tokens SHOULD expire after inactivity; RFC 10017 says authorization servers MUST cap the lifetime or expire after non-use for browser-based apps.

conflicts.topic: does refresh token rotation detect theft?
conflicts.note: RFC 9700 says rotation detects replay when both parties use the token; RFC 10017 says it is not sufficient when the attacker keeps the app from using the latest token, so no reuse is seen.
RFC 7519 makes aud OPTIONAL and requires rejection only when aud is present; RFC 9700 says access tokens SHOULD be audience-restricted and a resource server MUST refuse tokens not meant for it.

conflicts.topic: does revoking tokens stop access at once?
conflicts.note: RFC 10017 says revoking the access and/or refresh token suffices; RFC 7009 says access tokens are not immediately invalidated without access token revocation support, and self-contained ones need non-standard backend interaction.

RFC 9700 says XSS undermines sender-constrained tokens when the attacker gets the key material; RFC 10017 says DPoP with a non-extractable key prevents XSS exfiltration of usable tokens, but not a new flow.
